newsitem.title: USA: U.S. health panel sees possible pelvic disease risk.
newsitem.headline: U.S. health panel sees possible pelvic disease risk.

text.p: A U.S. health advisory panel on Tuesday said vaginal douching possibly was associated with two serious health problems for women, but that a direct link has not yet been established.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration panel said the practice was associated with risk of pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) and ectopic, or tubal, pregnancy but that studies so far had not proved a definite cause and effect.

"There might be something there, but we don't really have the data," said panel chairman Ralph D'Agostino of Boston University. Several panelists said they want the FDA to start regulating douches as drugs so that manufacturers would be forced to conduct safety and efficacy studies.

FDA does not require labeling for douches which are regulated as cosmetics. The industry voluntarily has included warnings and instructions but the panel said it wanted the FDA to act to ensure more consistency.
FDA official Michael Weintraub said the agency would take the committee's advice "to heart," but that the voluntary labeling seemed to work and was faster than any FDA process.
Douching is suspected in both PID and ectopic pregnancies because the practice seems to alter the natural balance of microorganisms, providing a pathway for disease.

SmithKline Beecham, maker of Massengill douches, is doing a year-long trial in which 3,000 participants are being assigned to receive either a disposable vinegar and water douche or a soft cloth for external cleansing. It may be a few years before all the results are in.
Some researchers at the meeting said women who use either commercial or homemade douches may be at risk for other reasons, such as high risk for sexually transmitted disease.
Millions of American women douche, either with home or commercial preparations. The Nonprescription Drug Manufacturers Association estimates that 230 million disposable douches were sold in 1996.
Sevgi Okten Aral of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said that as of 1995, one in four women douched.
